clusters.name: Your stepfather Desmond entering the household, 1987
clusters.reason: Around your stepfather moving in and your parents' separation over starting a family, you began secondary school: your distance from him, your pull toward your dad, anxiety over making the chess squad, and the tension in your parents' marriage all fell within the same year. Your mother's remarriage followed that autumn.

clusters.name: Your grandfather Gordon's death, 1989–1992
clusters.reason: Your grandfather died in June 1991, and within the two years before and after, your life shifted steadily. Your late nights began in 1989 as you settled in the rebuilt house with your stepfather's children; your mother filled in your college forms and you leaned hard on your roommate Rafe at conservatory. In October 1991 a wrist injury stopped your playing and you and Rafe clashed; you were high most days in your room, then lost and low by early 1992, unable to get going. Your grandmother had surgery for a thyroid tumour around the time your grandfather died. Each shift fell close to the next, building through the period, and no one else's story shows alongside yours in these months.

clusters.name: Your separation from Joelle, 1998–1999
clusters.reason: You bonded with Joelle in early 1998, and within eighteen months your insomnia began getting in the way before concerts, yet you were playing the best you had ever had and winning competitions. When you separated in the summer of 1999, you started with a therapist. The shifts are yours alone across these months.

clusters.name: Your grandmother Winifred's death from bowel cancer, 2001–2004
clusters.reason: Around your grandmother's death in early 2004, shifts piled up from late 2001. You ran out of steam for performing and your anxiety rose; your grandmother was found to have bowel cancer in 2001 or 2002; you had a disastrous audition and were done with performing. You grew distant from your family and friends, left Thornbury for Gull Harbour, then met Marisol and moved with her to Fenwick. When you and Marisol separated within the year, you sank into a deep depression once you were back in Thornbury, hardly moving from the sofa. Your grandmother spent her final months in your parents' home. Though you dropped in briefly on her sickroom on the way to the airport, you kept your distance, and you could not face your family. By early 2004 you had returned to your therapist and begun swimming laps; you requested help from your parents with therapy costs. Your grandmother died in February 2004.

clusters.name: Your grandmother Lorna's death, 2008
clusters.reason: Your grandmother died in January 2008, and within months your life shifted as you prepared for nursing school. At Alder Creek in July you were too drained for conversation with your mother, though she pressed to visit and you kept the door shut on her. In August you left for nursing school in Marlow Sound and stopped speaking to your mother; the silence held for roughly a year. Your aunt Imogen had a stroke in early 2009 with months of rehabilitation. The shifts cluster around your move and your grandmother's death, marking the break from your mother.

clusters.name: Your marriage to Wren, 2017–2019
clusters.reason: You married Wren in March 2017, and through late 2019 shifts accumulated around her family and your work. You saw your mother a bit less once Wren came along; your cousin Alice was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis; your sister Tara married and was expecting her first child; your aunt Imogen's memory was slipping and she lashed out when muddled. Your job steadied and paid well, easing your strain, yet your anxiety rose—constantly feeling you ought to be driving projects forward—and you started a sleeping pill. You aimed for shorter, more regular calls with your mother. In late October 2019, Wren was swamped one thing after another as her mother's retirement approached; you overfunctioned laying out a plan to settle her, and her family—her father, brother, and their two children—talked all day and nothing happened to one that the others didn't hear. Once the weekend had a plan Wren settled, yet at the lake house you awoke from the small hours with no more sleep and could only pull back as the others rose; you felt you didn't belong. Wren was anxious when you'd had no sleep at family occasions, and long quiet drives home followed. These shifts belonged together across the marriage and Wren's family's way of managing.
